| Dancer | Nationality | Notable Contributions / Roles |
|--------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **Marie Taglioni** (1815–1901) | Swedish | Pioneered the “en pointe” technique; star of *La Sylphide* (1832). Her ethereal style defined Romantic ballet. |

| **Fanny Elssler** (1810–1884) | Austrian | Virtuoso ballerina known for her virtuoso footwork and dramatic expressiveness; toured extensively in Europe and the United States. |
| **Marius Petipa** (1818–1910) | Russian (born French) | Dancer‑turned‑choreographer; created iconic ballets such as *Swan Lake* (1877), *The Sleeping Beauty* (1890), and *The Nutcracker* (1892). His choreography set the standard for classical ballet. |
| **Jean Coralli** (1797–1868) | French | Dancer and choreographer; co‑choreographer of *Giselle* (1841) and creator of many popular ballets of the era. |
| **Carlo Blasis** (1795–1865) | Italian | Renowned dancer‑teacher and author of *L’arte della danza* (1840), a foundational text on ballet technique and pedagogy. |
| **Anna Pavlova** (1889–1931) | Russian | Though her career peaked in the early 20th century, she was born in 1889 and began performing in the late 19th century. She became one of the most celebrated ballerinas of all time, known for her lyrical style and the iconic *The Dying Swan*. |
| **Martha Graham** (1894–1991) | American | While her major work emerged in the 20th century, she was born in 1894 and began training in the 1910s. Her early training and influences were rooted in the 19th‑century ballet tradition. |
| **Enrico Cecchetti** (1850–1928) | Italian | Dancer and teacher; developed the Cecchetti method, a rigorous ballet training system that remains influential worldwide. |
| **Adeline Genée** (1879–1961) | Danish | Prolific ballerina who performed across Europe and the U.S.; known for her technical precision and expressive artistry. |

These dancers were central to the development and popularization of ballet during the 19th century, each contributing uniquely to the art form’s evolution—whether through performance, choreography, or teaching.
